Singaporean youngsters are sophisticated meaning-makers who use texts of different modes (including comics, cartoons, video games, and television programmes) to construct their identities and negotiate the social worlds they inhabit.

Singaporean 10–12-year-olds are sophisticated meaning-makers who use texts to construct shifting subject positions and identities in their everyday lives and are able to do this because they are able to access a wide range of texts, including those that are ‘improper’ or ‘unsanctioned’.

the Singaporean 10–12-year-olds we interviewed are engaged in a range of informal literacies that are not always recognized or valued by their families or teachers, and that these informal literacies are not always aligned with the pedagogized literacy practices that are the focus of school.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are attempting to show that there is a great deal of knowledge about reading and writing that is not being recognized by educators, and we are arguing for its inclusion in literacy curricula.

we have been working with the idea that the Singaporean child is a complex being who is capable of multiple readings and interpretations of texts and of the social and cultural contexts in which they are embedded.

it shows how the Singaporean youngsters we have studied are engaged in a range of out-of-school practices with texts that are not only pleasurable and fun, but also productive of a range of competencies that are not easily recognized or acknowledged in schools.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we must listen carefully to the voices of young people in order to better understand the literacy practices they bring with them into school.

we should not be too quick to dismiss the value of the kinds of texts and activities that Singaporean youngsters like to read and do in their spare time, but instead, we should be open to learning from them.

we should listen to the voices of youngsters themselves as they talk with us about their everyday experiences and engagements with texts, and take them seriously as we seek to understand what they are up to in their lives.
